lessons.title: Student’s t and a single population mean
lessons.summary: Estimate an unknown variance, select the tail and distinguish evidence from proof.
lessons.objective: Carry out and interpret one-sample t-tests with the correct degrees of freedom.
lessons.before: Review sample means, variance, the normal distribution, hypotheses and significance levels.
lessons.ideas:
Estimating the variability

For n independent observations, the unbiased estimate of population variance is

\[s^2=\frac{\sum(x-\bar x)^2}{n-1}=\frac{\sum x^2-(\sum x)^2/n}{n-1}.\]

Here s is a sample standard deviation. The estimated standard error of the mean is s/√n; it describes variation between sample means, rather than between individual observations. Subtracting a coding constant changes the mean but leaves the variance unchanged.

Why a t distribution?

For a random sample from a normal population with unknown variance,

\[\begin{gathered}T=\frac{\bar X-\mu_0}{S/\sqrt n}\sim t_{n-1}\\\text{under }H_0:\mu=\mu_0.\end{gathered}\]

The extra uncertainty from estimating variance produces heavier tails than the standard normal distribution. The t distribution is symmetric about zero and approaches the standard normal as the degrees of freedom grow. A small sample size alone does not establish normality.

Choose the alternative before looking at the result

For H₁: μ>μ₀ use the upper tail; for μ<μ₀ use the lower tail. For μ≠μ₀ split the significance level equally between both tails. Write tν,p for the p-quantile, so P(T≤tν,p)=p. A two-sided p-value is twice the smaller tail probability.

Use the convention stated in the question. In this chapter reject when p≤α, including the critical boundary. Otherwise do not reject: this is insufficient evidence against the null, not proof that it is true. Express the conclusion about the population mean in the original units.
lessons.method:
1. Identify the population parameter and check random independent sampling and normality.
  2. State H₀ and a directional or two-sided H₁.
  3. Calculate s² and the standard error without early rounding.
  4. Calculate t and use n−1 degrees of freedom.
  5. Compare the correct tail with α, then conclude in context.
mistakes: Use n−1 in the unbiased variance, but √n in the standard error.
Do not use a two-sided critical value for a one-sided claim.
A negative statistic is not evidence in an upper-tail test.
Not rejecting a null does not prove it.

examples.title: 1 · Separate variance from standard error
examples.question: For a normal population, a random independent sample has n=9, Σx=108 and Σx²=1320. Find the mean, unbiased variance and estimated standard error.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\bar x=12\\s^2=\frac{1320-108^2/9}{8}=3\\\mathrm{SE}=\frac{\sqrt3}{3}.\end{gathered}\]

Variance has squared measurement units. The standard error has the same units as the mean.

examples.title: 2 · An upper-tail test
examples.question: Nine independently sampled normal processing times have mean 41 minutes and unbiased variance 9. Test H₀: μ=39 against H₁: μ>39 at 5%, using the supplied critical value 1.860.
examples.solution:
\[t=\frac{41-39}{3/\sqrt9}=2,\qquad\nu=8.\]

Since 2>1.860, reject H₀. There is sufficient evidence at 5% that the population mean processing time exceeds 39 minutes. The threshold is for an upper tail, not a central 95% interval.

examples.title: 3 · Both tails matter
examples.question: A normal population with unknown variance gives n=16, mean 17.5 and s²=4. Test μ=18 against μ≠18 at 5%, using the supplied positive critical value 2.131.
examples.solution:
\[t=\frac{17.5-18}{2/4}=-1,\qquad\nu=15.\]

The rejection region is t≤−2.131 or t≥2.131. The statistic lies between these limits, so do not reject. The data do not provide sufficient evidence of a difference from 18; they do not establish equality.

examples.title: 4 · Undo coding without changing the variance
examples.question: A sample of ten normal observations is coded by u=x−50. The summaries are Σu=8 and Σu²=20.8. Find the mean of x, its unbiased variance and the standard error.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\bar x=50+\frac8{10}=50.8\\s^2=\frac{20.8-8^2/10}{9}=\frac85\\\mathrm{SE}=\frac25.\end{gathered}\]

The added 50 belongs in the mean. It must not be added to the variance.

lessons.title: Independent means: the normal procedure
lessons.summary: Distinguish known population variances from large-sample estimated variances.
lessons.objective: Test a specified difference of independent population means with an appropriate normal model.
lessons.before: Review hypotheses and standard errors, independent random variables and the central limit theorem.
lessons.ideas:
Independence makes variances add

\[\operatorname{Var}(\bar X-\bar Y)=\frac{\sigma_X^2}{n_X}+\frac{\sigma_Y^2}{n_Y}.\]

Even though the sample means are subtracted, their variances add. This formula requires independent samples; it is not the formula for matched pairs.

Two routes to a normal statistic

If both populations are normal and their variances are known, use the known variances: the standardised difference is exactly normal at any sample sizes. If the variances are unknown but both samples are sufficiently large for the central limit approximation, estimate them separately by unbiased sample variances:

\[\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}=\sqrt{\frac{s_X^2}{n_X}+\frac{s_Y^2}{n_Y}},\qquad z=\frac{(\bar x-\bar y)-\delta_0}{\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}}.\]

The latter procedure is approximate, needs independent random samples with finite population variances and does not require equal variances. Sample size does not cure a biased or dependent sampling scheme. For small independent normal samples with a common unknown variance, use the pooled t procedure instead.

A non-zero null difference

To investigate whether A exceeds B by more than 2 units, use H₀: μA−μB=2 and H₁: μA−μB>2, not a null of zero. Retain the same order of subtraction throughout. Reversing a contrast reverses its statistic and alternative together.

Significance as a range

If α is expressed in percent and the calculated p-value is p, rejection occurs for 100p≤α<100 under the stated boundary convention. Non-rejection occurs for 0<α<100p. Compare probabilities with probabilities, not with percentages.
lessons.method:
1. Define the order of the population mean difference.
  2. Check whether variances are known or are being estimated with a large-sample approximation.
  3. Add the variances of the two sample means.
  4. Subtract the hypothesised difference and standardise.
  5. Use the appropriate normal tail and report the evidence in context.
mistakes: Subtract means, but add their variance contributions.
Do not pool unequal unknown variances merely because samples are large.
Subtract the non-zero null difference when one is stated.
A significance level of 5% is the probability 0.05.

examples.title: 1 · Known variances and an exact normal model
examples.question: Independent normal populations have known variances 9 and 16. Samples of sizes 9 and 16 have means 14 and 12. Find the standard error and the z statistic for equal population means.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\mathrm{SE}=\sqrt{9/9+16/16}=\sqrt2\\z=\frac2{\sqrt2}=\sqrt2.\end{gathered}\]

The normal model is exact because the populations are normal and the variances are known. No t degrees of freedom are needed.

examples.title: 2 · Unknown variances, large samples
examples.question: Independent random samples have nA=64, nB=100, means 23 and 22, and unbiased variance estimates 16 and 25. Use a large-sample normal approximation to test equal means against different means at 5%, using 1.960.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}=\sqrt{16/64+25/100}=\frac1{\sqrt2}\\z=\sqrt2.\end{gathered}\]

Since |z|<1.960, do not reject. There is insufficient evidence of different population means. Neither equal population variances nor normal individual observations were assumed; the approximation uses the independent large samples.

examples.title: 3 · A minimum useful difference
examples.question: Independent large samples give means 8.4 and 7.2 and an estimated standard error of 0.4. Test whether μA−μB exceeds 0.5 at 5%, using the supplied upper-tail critical value 1.645.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}H_0:\mu_A-\mu_B=0.5\\H_1:\mu_A-\mu_B>0.5\\z=\frac{1.2-0.5}{0.4}=1.75.\end{gathered}\]

Reject H₀ since 1.75>1.645. The evidence concerns a gain above 0.5, not simply a gain above zero.

examples.title: 4 · A p-value determines the whole range
examples.question: A one-sided normal test has calculated p-value 0.032. With α measured in percent, for which levels is H₀ rejected? The rule is p≤α/100.
examples.solution: The range is \(3.2\le\alpha<100\). At 1% do not reject; at 5% reject. The boundary 3.2% is included because equality is in the rejection rule.

lessons.title: Pooled variance and independent-sample t-tests
lessons.summary: Weight two variance estimates by their degrees of freedom before comparing means.
lessons.objective: Calculate a common variance estimate and use a two-sample t statistic with the correct assumptions.
lessons.before: Review unbiased variance and independent means. Know the difference between independent and paired observations.
lessons.ideas:
Pooling has an assumption

For independent random samples from two normal populations with the same unknown population variance, combine the centred sums of squares:

\[s_p^2=\frac{(n_X-1)s_X^2+(n_Y-1)s_Y^2}{n_X+n_Y-2}.\]

This is a degrees-of-freedom weighted estimate of a common variance. It is not generally the arithmetic average of two sample variances. Normality and a common population variance must be given or justified; similar observed variances alone do not establish either condition.

Standardise the difference

\[t=\frac{(\bar x-\bar y)-\delta_0}{s_p\sqrt{1/n_X+1/n_Y}},\qquad\nu=n_X+n_Y-2.\]

Under the null this statistic has a t distribution with ν degrees of freedom. The denominator uses the square root of the pooled variance. Choose the one- or two-sided critical value from the alternative, not from whether the observed difference happens to be positive.

Reconstructing missing information

A stated pooled variance may give an equation for an unknown sample size. After solving, check sample sizes are integers, exceed 1 and produce non-negative centred sums of squares. An algebraic root outside that domain is not a possible sample size. To estimate the common standard deviation, take the square root only after pooling the variances.
lessons.method:
1. Check independent samples, normal populations and a common unknown variance.
  2. Find each mean and centred sum of squares.
  3. Pool the centred sums using the combined degrees of freedom.
  4. Calculate the standard error and t statistic for the stated null.
  5. Use nX+nY−2 degrees of freedom and conclude in context.
mistakes: Pooling standard deviations is not pooling variances.
Weight by n−1, not n.
Use the two-sample degrees of freedom, not the smaller sample size minus one.
Equal variances do not make paired observations independent.

examples.title: 1 · Unequal sizes require unequal weights
examples.question: Independent samples of sizes 6 and 10 have unbiased variances 4 and 8. Their populations share a variance. Estimate the common variance and standard deviation.
examples.solution:
\[s_p^2=\frac{5(4)+9(8)}{14}=\frac{46}{7},\qquad\widehat\sigma=\sqrt{\frac{46}{7}}.\]

The unweighted average 6 would be incorrect.

examples.title: 2 · From pooling to a conclusion
examples.question: Independent normal samples have sizes 5 and 5, means 18 and 16, and unbiased variances 2 and 3. Assume a common unknown variance. Test equality against a positive A−B difference at 5%, using 1.860.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}s_p^2=\frac{4(2)+4(3)}8=\frac52\\\mathrm{SE}=\sqrt{\frac52\left(\frac15+\frac15\right)}=1\\t=2.\end{gathered}\]

There are 8 degrees of freedom. Since 2>1.860, reject H₀: there is sufficient evidence of a greater population mean for A.

examples.title: 3 · A specified non-zero difference
examples.question: Independent normal samples from equal-variance populations have sizes 8 and 8, means 12.5 and 11, and unbiased variances 4 and 4. Find the statistic for H₀: μA−μB=0.5.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}s_p^2=4\\\mathrm{SE}=\sqrt{4(1/8+1/8)}=1\\t=\frac{1.5-0.5}{1}=1\\\nu=14.\end{gathered}\]

The appropriate critical tail would depend on the stated alternative.

examples.title: 4 · Recover a missing variance
examples.question: Samples of sizes 7 and 11 have pooled variance 5. The first unbiased sample variance is 3. Find the second unbiased variance.
examples.solution:
\[16(5)=6(3)+10s_Y^2,\qquad s_Y^2=\frac{31}{5}.\]

The estimate is positive. Both the numerator weights and the denominator come from degrees of freedom.

lessons.title: Paired observations and mean differences
lessons.summary: Keep the matching, define the direction and analyse one sample of differences.
lessons.objective: Carry out paired t-tests and identify which normality and independence assumptions are required.
lessons.before: Review one-sample t-tests. Put both readings in the same units before subtraction.
lessons.ideas:
The pair is the unit of analysis

Before-and-after measurements on the same object are dependent. Matched pairs may also be formed before random allocation. Define d consistently, for example before minus after when positive means a reduction. There are n differences from n pairs, even though there are 2n readings.

\[\bar d=\frac{\sum d}{n},\qquad s_d^2=\frac{\sum d^2-(\sum d)^2/n}{n-1},\qquad t=\frac{\bar d-\delta_0}{s_d/\sqrt n}.\]

Use n−1 degrees of freedom. The normality assumption concerns the population of differences, not necessarily each original population. Different pairs must be independent, while the two readings within each pair need not be.

Do not discard the cross-product

\[\begin{gathered}\sum d=\sum x-\sum y,\qquad\sum d^2=\sum x^2+\sum y^2-2\sum xy\\(d=x-y).\end{gathered}\]

Subtracting the two sample variances ignores the dependence. If only summary data are given, the cross-product supplies the missing information. Adding the same correction to both readings in a pair leaves its difference unchanged.

Interpret direction and assumptions

If d=before−after, a claim of a reduction greater than c uses H₁: μd>c. If you reverse d, also reverse the null value and alternative. A strong outlier or skew in a small sample makes the normal-difference model questionable. A sign test for a population median is a different procedure and parameter; it is not a t-test for the mean.
lessons.method:
1. Identify the matching and convert to common units.
  2. Define the signed within-pair difference.
  3. Find its mean and unbiased variance, retaining all pairs.
  4. Apply a one-sample t-test to those differences.
  5. State assumptions about the differences and interpret the sign in context.
mistakes: Use n pairs, not 2n separate observations.
Normality is required for the population of differences.
Do not pool the original sample variances for paired data.
Changing minutes to seconds must precede subtraction.

examples.title: 1 · Work with five differences
examples.question: Five independent matched pairs give before-minus-after differences 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Find their mean, unbiased variance and standard error.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\bar d=3\\s_d^2=\frac{55-15^2/5}{4}=\frac52\\\mathrm{SE}=\frac1{\sqrt2}.\end{gathered}\]

There are five observations in the difference sample, not ten.

examples.title: 2 · Use cross-products
examples.question: For six independent pairs, Σx=120, Σy=108, Σx²=2420, Σy²=1964 and Σxy=2174. Find the mean and unbiased variance of d=x−y.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\sum d=12\\\sum d^2=2420+1964-2(2174)=36\\\bar d=2\\s_d^2=\frac{36-12^2/6}{5}=\frac{12}{5}.\end{gathered}\]

The cross-product must be included.

examples.title: 3 · Test an improvement threshold
examples.question: For nine independent pairs, the normal population of before-minus-after differences has unknown variance. The sample gives mean 1.4 and s²=0.81. Test whether the population mean reduction exceeds 0.8 at 5%, using 1.860.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}H_0:\mu_d=0.8\\H_1:\mu_d>0.8\\t=\frac{1.4-0.8}{0.9/3}=2\\\nu=8.\end{gathered}\]

Reject H₀. There is sufficient evidence of a population mean reduction greater than 0.8 units, assuming normal differences and independent pairs.

examples.title: 4 · Convert units before pairing
examples.question: A task takes 5 minutes before a change and 270 seconds afterwards. Find the reduction in minutes. What happens if both readings for this pair were recorded 6 seconds too high?
examples.solution: The after time is 270/60=4.5 minutes, so the reduction is 0.5 minutes. Correcting both readings subtracts 0.1 minute from each. Their difference remains 0.5, so the paired statistic is unchanged.

lessons.title: Confidence intervals for one mean
lessons.summary: Construct, interpret and reverse an interval without confusing a mean with individual readings.
lessons.objective: Find t intervals for a population mean and reconstruct sample summaries from a supplied interval.
lessons.before: Review unbiased variance and t quantiles. For paired means apply the same method to differences.
lessons.ideas:
Estimate plus or minus uncertainty

For independent random observations from a normal population with unknown variance, a central 100(1−α)% interval is

\[\bar x\pm t_{n-1,1-\alpha/2}\frac{s}{\sqrt n}.\]

Use a two-sided critical value and give both endpoints, units and confidence level. Keep full precision until the requested final rounding. If the population variance is known, a normal-population mean instead uses σ/√n with a normal critical value.

What confidence means

The population mean is fixed. Under repeated independent random sampling, the stated percentage of intervals produced by this procedure would contain it. The interval is not a range containing that percentage of individual observations. Dependence, selection bias or an incorrect normal model can invalidate its advertised coverage.

Reverse the construction

For endpoints L and U, let m=(L+U)/2 and h=(U−L)/2. When the supplied critical value c is to be treated as exact,

\[\begin{gathered}\bar x=m\\s^2=n\left(\frac h c\right)^2\\\sum x=n\bar x\\\sum x^2=(n-1)s^2+n\bar x^2.\end{gathered}\]

Use the critical value stated in the problem for a reverse calculation; replacing a tabulated value by a more precise quantile changes the problem's data. An interval based on rounded endpoints may otherwise not determine exact summaries.

Connect tests and intervals carefully

A central 100(1−α)% interval corresponds to a two-sided α test under the same model. Interior values are not rejected. At an endpoint, follow the stated equality convention: when p≤α is rejected, that boundary value is rejected. A central 95% interval does not directly supply a one-sided 5% test.
lessons.method:
1. Identify the parameter, model and standard error.
  2. Find the two-sided t quantile with n−1 degrees of freedom.
  3. Calculate the margin and both endpoints, rounding only at the end.
  4. For reverse questions use the midpoint and half-width first.
  5. Interpret repeated-sampling coverage and check any requested test has the matching tails.
mistakes: The confidence level concerns the procedure, not the proportion of individual observations.
A 95% interval uses 2.5% in each tail.
Do not replace a supplied exact tabulated value in a reverse problem.
Give both endpoints in increasing order.

examples.title: 1 · An interval using a supplied critical value
examples.question: For a normal population with unknown variance, n=9, sample mean 30 and s²=9. Construct the interval using the supplied central critical value 2.306, treating it as exact.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\mathrm{SE}=1\\30\pm2.306=(27.694,32.306).\end{gathered}\]

For a central 95% t interval there are 8 degrees of freedom. Both endpoints are required; the mean alone is not the interval.

examples.title: 2 · Recover the variance
examples.question: A t interval for a normal mean from n=16 has endpoints 20 and 24. It used the supplied critical value 2 exactly. Recover the sample mean, unbiased variance, Σx and Σx².
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\bar x=22\\h=2\\s^2=16(2/2)^2=16\\\sum x=352\\\sum x^2=15(16)+16(22)^2=7984.\end{gathered}\]

The stipulated critical value is data for this reconstruction, not a value to recalculate.

examples.title: 3 · Reverse an interval for a paired mean
examples.question: An interval for a population mean reduction from nine independent normal differences is (0.4,1.6), calculated with the stipulated critical value 2. Recover the mean and unbiased variance of the differences.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\bar d=1\\h=0.6\\s_d^2=9(0.6/2)^2=\frac{81}{100}.\end{gathered}\]

These summaries describe the differences, not either original sample separately.

examples.title: 4 · Solve a rejection boundary
examples.question: A normal sample gives n=9, mean 14 and s²=9. An upper-tail t test uses critical value c=2. Find all null values k rejected by H₁: μ>k, including the critical boundary.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\frac{14-k}{1}\ge2\\\Longleftrightarrow\\k\le12.\end{gathered}\]

Smaller proposed means are contradicted in the upper direction. Under the stated rule k=12 is rejected as well.

lessons.title: Confidence intervals for differences of means
lessons.summary: Select a normal, pooled t or paired interval and preserve the order of subtraction.
lessons.objective: Construct complete intervals for population mean contrasts and use them to interpret compatible tests.
lessons.ideas:
Start with the design, not a memorised critical value

For independent populations with known variances and normal sample means, use

\[(\bar x-\bar y)\pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\sigma_X^2/n_X+\sigma_Y^2/n_Y}.\]

This is exact for normal populations with known variances. For independent large samples with unknown finite variances, substitute separate unbiased variance estimates; the interval is then a normal approximation and needs no equal-variance assumption.

Small normal samples with a common unknown variance

\[(\bar x-\bar y)\pm t_{n_X+n_Y-2,1-\alpha/2}\,s_p\sqrt{1/n_X+1/n_Y}.\]

Pool only when a common population variance is assumed. For matched pairs use the one-mean t interval for the differences, with n−1 degrees of freedom. Pairing and pooling are different designs.

Reverse an interval correctly

If (L,U) estimates μA−μB, then (−U,−L) estimates μB−μA at the same confidence level. Negating without reversing the endpoints produces an incorrectly ordered interval.

Interpret the whole interval

An interval wholly above zero supports a positive difference in population means, not a claim that every A observation exceeds every B observation. An interval with zero strictly inside is compatible with equality for the matching two-sided test; it does not prove equality. An interval wholly below zero supports the opposite direction. Use the same model, confidence level and boundary convention for a test comparison. A one-sided improvement threshold requires its own tail calculation.
lessons.method:
1. Define the contrast and identify independent or paired data.
  2. Select known-variance normal, large-sample normal, pooled t or paired t.
  3. Find its standard error and central critical value.
  4. Give both endpoints in the stated order and units.
  5. Interpret the parameter difference and any matching two-sided test.
mistakes: Small samples do not require t when normal-population variances are known.
Use (−U,−L) when reversing the contrast.
Zero inside an interval does not prove equal means.
The interval concerns means, not every individual comparison.

examples.title: 1 · A large-sample interval
examples.question: Independent large samples have sizes 100 and 100, means 51 and 50, and unbiased variances 9 and 16. Construct an approximate 95% interval for μA−μB using 1.960 exactly.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}=\sqrt{9/100+16/100}=\frac12\\1\pm1.960(1/2)=(0.020,1.980).\end{gathered}\]

The interval is positive. The corresponding two-sided 5% normal-approximation test rejects equality; no equal-variance assumption was needed.

examples.title: 2 · A pooled t interval
examples.question: Independent normal samples have sizes 5 and 5, means 10 and 9, and unbiased variances 2 and 3. Assume a common variance. Use the supplied central critical value 2.306 to construct the interval.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}s_p^2=5/2\\\mathrm{SE}=1\\\nu=8\\1\pm2.306=(-1.306,3.306).\end{gathered}\]

Zero is inside. Do not reject equality in the corresponding two-sided test, but do not claim the means are equal.

examples.title: 3 · Small samples with known variances
examples.question: Two independent normal populations have known variances 4 and 9. Samples of sizes 16 and 36 have means 8 and 7. Use the supplied normal critical value 1.645 for a central 90% interval.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\mathrm{SE}=\sqrt{4/16+9/36}=\frac1{\sqrt2}\\\left(1-\frac{1.645}{\sqrt2},\ 1+\frac{1.645}{\sqrt2}\right).\end{gathered}\]

The known population variances make the normal procedure appropriate despite small samples. The stipulated rounded critical value is used as supplied.

examples.title: 4 · Change the order of the contrast
examples.question: A central interval for μA−μB is (−3.4,−0.8). Give the corresponding interval for μB−μA and interpret its sign.
examples.solution: The reversed interval is (0.8,3.4). Both endpoints are positive, supporting a greater population mean for B under the model. This says nothing about every possible pair of individual observations.

questions.title: Mean, variance and standard error
questions.prompt_html: A random sample has \(n=9\), \(\sum u=72\), \(\sum u^2=596\), where \(x=u+0\). Find the mean of x, its unbiased variance and the estimated standard error of its mean, exactly.
questions.answer_html: Sample mean: \(8\); Unbiased variance: \(\frac{5}{2}\); Standard error: \(\frac{\sqrt{10}}{6}\)
questions.solution_html: Use the coded mean plus the offset. Calculate \(s^2=[\sum u^2-(\sum u)^2/n]/(n-1)\) and then \(s/\sqrt n\). Adding a constant leaves the variance unchanged.
questions.hint_html: Identify the sampling design, parameter and tail before calculating. Keep all requested quantities, use the stated critical value and round only when instructed.

questions.title: Mean, variance and standard error
questions.prompt_html: A random sample has \(n=10\), \(\sum u=12\), \(\sum u^2=\frac{234}{5}\), where \(x=u+30\). Find the mean of x, its unbiased variance and the estimated standard error of its mean, exactly.
questions.answer_html: Sample mean: \(\frac{156}{5}\); Unbiased variance: \(\frac{18}{5}\); Standard error: \(\frac{3}{5}\)
questions.solution_html: Use the coded mean plus the offset. Calculate \(s^2=[\sum u^2-(\sum u)^2/n]/(n-1)\) and then \(s/\sqrt n\). Adding a constant leaves the variance unchanged.
questions.hint_html: Identify the sampling design, parameter and tail before calculating. Keep all requested quantities, use the stated critical value and round only when instructed.

questions.title: The complete one-sample statistic
questions.prompt_html: A random independent sample from a normal population with unknown variance has \(n=9\), \(\bar x=32\) and \(s^2=9\). For \(H_0:\mu=30\), give the t statistic and its degrees of freedom exactly.
questions.answer_html: Test statistic: \(2\); Degrees of freedom: \(8\)
questions.solution_html: Standardise the difference from the null by \(s/\sqrt n\), retaining its sign. There are n−1 degrees of freedom.
questions.hint_html: Identify the sampling design, parameter and tail before calculating. Keep all requested quantities, use the stated critical value and round only when instructed.

questions.title: The complete one-sample statistic
questions.prompt_html: A random independent sample from a normal population with unknown variance has \(n=16\), \(\bar x=\frac{31}{2}\) and \(s^2=4\). For \(H_0:\mu=16\), give the t statistic and its degrees of freedom exactly.
questions.answer_html: Test statistic: \(-1\); Degrees of freedom: \(15\)
questions.solution_html: Standardise the difference from the null by \(s/\sqrt n\), retaining its sign. There are n−1 degrees of freedom.
questions.hint_html: Identify the sampling design, parameter and tail before calculating. Keep all requested quantities, use the stated critical value and round only when instructed.

questions.title: An upper-tail boundary
questions.prompt_html: A normal sample gives \(n=9\), \(\bar x=18\), \(s^2=9\). Test \(H_0:\mu=k\) against \(H_1:\mu>k\), rejecting at \(t\ge c\). Use the stipulated critical value \(c=2\) exactly. Rejection is \(k\le B\). Find B.
questions.answer_html: Largest rejected null value: \(16\)
questions.solution_html: Rearrange \((\bar x-k)/(s/\sqrt n)\ge c\), giving \(k\le\bar x-cs/\sqrt n\). Equality is included as stated.
questions.hint_html: Identify the sampling design, parameter and tail before calculating. Keep all requested quantities, use the stated critical value and round only when instructed.

marking_criteria.description_html: Give the correct largest rejected null value.

questions.title: An upper-tail boundary
questions.prompt_html: A normal sample gives \(n=16\), \(\bar x=21\), \(s^2=16\). Test \(H_0:\mu=k\) against \(H_1:\mu>k\), rejecting at \(t\ge c\). Use the stipulated critical value \(c=\frac{3}{2}\) exactly. Rejection is \(k\le B\). Find B.
questions.answer_html: Largest rejected null value: \(\frac{39}{2}\)
questions.solution_html: Rearrange \((\bar x-k)/(s/\sqrt n)\ge c\), giving \(k\le\bar x-cs/\sqrt n\). Equality is included as stated.
questions.hint_html: Identify the sampling design, parameter and tail before calculating. Keep all requested quantities, use the stated critical value and round only when instructed.

The mass of sealant delivered by a dispenser is measured in grams. The engineer suspects that its population mean exceeds 250.5 g. A random sample of 9 independent measurements is obtained.

The underlying population is normal; its variance is unknown.

  1. Carry out an appropriate test at the 5% significance level of the claim that the population mean exceeds 250.5 g. State your hypotheses and give a conclusion in context.

questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(t=1.973\) with \(\nu=8\). There is sufficient evidence at the 5% level that the population mean exceeds 250.5 g.

(b)

\((250.316,\ 252.862)\) g.
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Let \(\mu\) denote the relevant population mean.

\[H_0:\mu=250.5,\qquad H_1:\mu>250.5.\]

Using the unbiased variance estimate,

\[\bar{x}=\frac{2264.3}{9}=251.588889,\]
\[s^2=\frac{\sum x^2-(\sum x)^2/9}{8}=\frac{21.9288889}{8}=2.74111111.\]
\[\mathrm{SE}=\frac{s}{\sqrt{9}}=0.551876708.\]

Under \(H_0\), the test statistic has a \(t_{8}\) distribution.

\[t=\frac{\text{sample estimate}-\text{null value}}{\mathrm{SE}}=\frac{251.58889-(250.5)}{0.55187671}=1.973.\]

The 5% one-sided rejection region is \(t\ge 1.860\).

Since \(1.973\ge 1.860\), reject \(H_0\). There is sufficient evidence at the 5% level that the population mean exceeds 250.5 g.

(b)

Use an equal-tailed 95% confidence interval for \(\mu\).

\[t_{8,0.975}\approx 2.306,\qquad\text{interval}=\text{estimate}\pm c\,\mathrm{SE}.\]
\[251.58889\pm 2.306004\times 0.55187671=251.58889\pm 1.27263.\]

The interval is \((250.316,\ 252.862)\) g.

The population variance is unknown: using a standard normal critical value instead of the \(t\) critical value would not be the specified small-sample procedure.

Nine machines are independently selected at random. Each is measured before and after a maintenance procedure. Their start-up times, in seconds, are

Pair123456789
Before303642485460667278
After29.836.341.547.253.758.864.57166

For part (a) only, assume that the population of reductions is normally distributed.

  1. Carry out an appropriate test at the 5% significance level of the claim that the population mean reduction is positive. State your hypotheses and give a conclusion in context.

    [6]

  2. A larger investigation shows that the population of reductions is strongly right-skewed. Explain why the test in part (a) is then questionable.

    [2]

  3. Name a simple non-parametric test for whether the population median reduction is positive when neither normality nor symmetry can be assumed. No calculation is required.

    [1]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(t=1.500\) with \(\nu=8\). There is insufficient evidence at the 5% level that the population mean reduction is positive.

(b)

The normality assumption for the population of paired differences is doubtful.

(c)

A paired-sample sign test, applied to the reductions.
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Let \(\mu_d\) denote the relevant population mean difference.

\[H_0:\mu_d=0,\qquad H_1:\mu_d>0.\]

Keep each pair together and define \(d=\text{before}-\text{after}\).

\[d:\quad 0.2,\ -0.3,\ 0.5,\ 0.8,\ 0.3,\ 1.2,\ 1.5,\ 1,\ 12.\]

Using the unbiased variance estimate,

\[\bar{d}=\frac{17.2}{9}=1.91111111,\]
\[s_d^2=\frac{\sum d^2-(\sum d)^2/9}{8}=\frac{116.928889}{8}=14.6161111.\]
\[\mathrm{SE}=\frac{s_d}{\sqrt{9}}=1.27436743.\]

Under \(H_0\), the test statistic has a \(t_{8}\) distribution.

\[t=\frac{\text{sample estimate}-\text{null value}}{\mathrm{SE}}=\frac{1.9111111-(0)}{1.2743674}=1.500.\]

The 5% one-sided rejection region is \(t\ge 1.860\).

Since \(1.500<1.860\), do not reject \(H_0\). There is insufficient evidence at the 5% level that the population mean reduction is positive.

(b)

Strong right-skewness of the population of differences contradicts the normality assumption required for this exact small-sample paired t procedure. A large positive difference can also strongly affect the mean and standard deviation. The mere fact that the reduction depends on the initial time would not, by itself, prove non-normality.

(c)

A paired-sample sign test can target the population median reduction. It does not test the same population-mean claim as part (a); a change of target must be stated.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Identify the population parameter and the direction of the claim before selecting the critical tail.

(b)

Normality is required for the differences, not separately for both columns.

(c)

The proposed replacement concerns a median, not a mean.

marking_criteria.description_html: Obtain the required sample statistics with unbiased variance(s).
There is insufficient evidence at the 5% level that the population mean reduction is positive.
Identify the population of differences as the relevant distribution.

questions.title: Matched-pair allocation and a recording correction
questions.prompt_html:
Twenty filter cartridges are arranged into ten matched pairs with similar measured capacity. Within each pair, one cartridge is randomly assigned to process X and the other to process Y. The volume filtered before replacement, in litres, is recorded.

Pair12345678910
Process X63756782705879736877
Process Y66767180756079797081

Different matched pairs are independent. The manufacturer claims that process Y increases the population mean filtered volume.

  1. Carry out an appropriate test at the 1% significance level of the claim that process Y has a positive population mean gain relative to X within matched pairs. State your hypotheses and give a conclusion in context.

    [7]

  2. State an assumption needed for the procedure to be valid.

    [1]

  3. For pair 4, both recorded volumes were 3 litres too high. Explain whether correcting this error changes the test statistic or conclusion in part (a).

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(t=3.273\) with \(\nu=9\). There is sufficient evidence at the 1% level that process Y has a positive population mean gain relative to X within matched pairs.

(b)

The population of within-pair differences is normally distributed, and different pairs are independent.

(c)

Neither the test statistic nor the conclusion changes.
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Let \(\mu_d\) denote the relevant population mean difference.

\[H_0:\mu_d=0,\qquad H_1:\mu_d>0.\]

Keep each pair together and define \(d=\text{Y}-\text{X}\).

\[d:\quad 3,\ 1,\ 4,\ -2,\ 5,\ 2,\ 0,\ 6,\ 2,\ 4.\]

Using the unbiased variance estimate,

\[\bar{d}=\frac{25}{10}=2.5,\]
\[s_d^2=\frac{\sum d^2-(\sum d)^2/10}{9}=\frac{52.5}{9}=5.83333333.\]
\[\mathrm{SE}=\frac{s_d}{\sqrt{10}}=0.763762616.\]

Under \(H_0\), the test statistic has a \(t_{9}\) distribution.

\[t=\frac{\text{sample estimate}-\text{null value}}{\mathrm{SE}}=\frac{2.5-(0)}{0.76376262}=3.273.\]

The 1% one-sided rejection region is \(t\ge 2.821\).

Since \(3.273\ge 2.821\), reject \(H_0\). There is sufficient evidence at the 1% level that process Y has a positive population mean gain relative to X within matched pairs.

(b)

The population of within-pair differences is normally distributed, and different pairs are independent.

(c)

The pair-4 difference remains \((80-3)-(82-3)=80-82=-2\). All ten differences, their mean and their variance are unchanged; so the paired t statistic and conclusion are unchanged.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Identify the population parameter and the direction of the claim before selecting the critical tail.

(b)

State an assumption about the population or the sampling scheme, not that the observed data must be exactly normal.

(c)

Recompute the difference, not the two column means separately.

questions.title: Recovering a sum of squares from an interval
questions.prompt_html:
The quantity of interest is the length of a manufactured pin, in millimetres.

A random sample of 10 independent observations is taken from a normal population with unknown variance. A 95% confidence interval for its mean is reported as \([48.3,51.1]\).

This interval was calculated using the tabulated critical value \(t=2.262\). Treat the endpoints and this tabulated value as exact when reversing the calculation.

  1. For the sample used to construct the stated confidence interval, find an unbiased estimate of the population variance.

    [4]

  2. Find the sum of the squared sample measurements.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[s_x^2=3.830635862.\]

(b)

\[\sum x^2=24735.37572.\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The interval is symmetric about the sample mean, and its half-width is \(h\).

\[\bar{x}=\frac{48.3+51.1}{2}=49.7,\qquad h=\frac{51.1-48.3}{2}=1.4.\]
\[h=t\frac{s}{\sqrt n}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad s^2=n\left(\frac{h}{t}\right)^2=10\left(\frac{1.4}{2.262}\right)^2=3.830635862.\]

(b)

\[\sum x^2=(n-1)s^2+n\bar x^2=9(3.830635862)+10(49.7)^2=24735.37572.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use the interval midpoint and half-width. In the variance formula, distinguish \(\sum x^2\) from \(\sum(x-\bar x)^2\).

(b)

The sum of squares is the centred sum of squares plus \(n\bar x^2\).

questions.title: A 99% interval and a non-rejection range
questions.prompt_html:
The mass x, in grams, of an independently selected packet has a normal distribution with mean \(\mu\) and unknown variance. A random sample of 11 packets gives

\[\sum x=2215.4,\qquad\sum x^2=446244.06.\]

  1. Find a 99% confidence interval for the population mean \(\mu\), giving both endpoints to 3 decimal places.

    [4]

  2. Find the range of values of \(k\) for which a 5% one-sided \(t\)-test of \(H_0:\mu=k\) against \(H_1:\mu<k\) does not reject \(H_0\). Include the critical boundary in the rejection region.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\((199.011,\ 203.789)\) g.

(b)

\[k<B,\qquad B=\frac{1007}{5} + t_{10,0.95}\sqrt{\frac{25}{44}}.\]

Numerically, \(B\approx 202.7662\).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Using the unbiased variance estimate,

\[\bar{x}=\frac{2215.4}{11}=201.4,\]
\[s^2=\frac{\sum x^2-(\sum x)^2/11}{10}=\frac{62.5}{10}=6.25.\]
\[\mathrm{SE}=\frac{s}{\sqrt{11}}=0.753778361.\]

Use an equal-tailed 99% confidence interval for \(\mu\).

\[t_{10,0.995}\approx 3.169,\qquad\text{interval}=\text{estimate}\pm c\,\mathrm{SE}.\]
\[201.4\pm 3.169273\times 0.75377836=201.4\pm 2.3889292.\]

The interval is \((199.011,\ 203.789)\) g.

The population variance is unknown: using a standard normal critical value instead of the \(t\) critical value would not be the specified small-sample procedure.

(b)

Use \(H_0:\mu=k\), \(H_1:\mu<k\) with \(\nu=10\).

\[t=\frac{201.4-k}{0.753778361}.\]

The positive critical value is \(c=t_{10,0.95}\approx 1.812\). Including equality in the rejection region, the required condition is

\[t>-1.812.\]
\[k<B,\quad B=\frac{1007}{5} + t_{10,0.95}\sqrt{\frac{25}{44}}.\]
\[k<B,\qquad B=\frac{1007}{5} + t_{10,0.95}\sqrt{\frac{25}{44}}.\]

Numerically, \(B\approx 202.7662\).

The boundary is excluded because equality belongs to the rejection region. The rounded decimal is not an exact cutoff; use the expression above at a boundary.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

A two-sided confidence interval leaves half of the excluded probability in each tail.

(b)

Write the test statistic in terms of \(k\) and solve the rejection or non-rejection inequality.

questions.title: Recovering an interval before comparing algorithms
questions.prompt_html:
The durations of audio segments generated by two algorithms are measured in minutes. For algorithm A:

A random sample of 9 independent observations is taken from a normal population with unknown variance. A 95% confidence interval for its mean is reported as \([2.71,3.09]\).

This interval was calculated using the tabulated critical value \(t=2.306\). Treat the endpoints and this tabulated value as exact when reversing the calculation.

An independent sample of 11 segments from algorithm B gives

\[\sum y=34.32,\qquad\sum y^2=107.5624.\]

Both duration distributions are normal with the same unknown variance. Let \(\mu_A,\mu_B\) denote their population means.

  1. For the sample used to construct the stated confidence interval, recover \(\sum x\) and \(\sum x^2\) for this sample.

    [5]

  2. Carry out an appropriate test at the 5% significance level of the claim that algorithm B has a greater population mean segment duration than algorithm A. State your hypotheses and give a conclusion in context.

    [8]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\sum x=26.1,\qquad\sum x^2=76.17878863.\]

(b)

\(t=2.105\) with \(\nu=18\). There is sufficient evidence at the 5% level that algorithm B has a greater population mean segment duration than algorithm A.
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The interval is symmetric about the sample mean, and its half-width is \(h\).

\[\bar{x}=\frac{2.71+3.09}{2}=2.9,\qquad h=\frac{3.09-2.71}{2}=0.19.\]
\[h=t\frac{s}{\sqrt n}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad s^2=n\left(\frac{h}{t}\right)^2=9\left(\frac{0.19}{2.306}\right)^2=0.06109857839.\]
\[\sum x=n\bar{x}=26.1,\]
\[\sum x^2=(n-1)s_x^2+n\bar{x}^2=76.17878863.\]

(b)

Let \(\mu_B-\mu_A\) denote the relevant population mean difference.

\[H_0:\mu_B-\mu_A=0,\qquad H_1:\mu_B-\mu_A>0.\]

Using the unbiased variance estimate,

\[\bar{x}=\frac{26.1}{9}=2.9,\]
\[s^2=\frac{\sum x^2-(\sum x)^2/9}{8}=\frac{0.488788627}{8}=0.0610985784.\]

Using the unbiased variance estimate,

\[\bar{y}=\frac{34.32}{11}=3.12,\]
\[s_y^2=\frac{\sum y^2-(\sum y)^2/11}{10}=\frac{0.484}{10}=0.0484.\]
\[s_p^2=\frac{(8)s_x^2+(10)s_y^2}{18}=\frac{0.488788627+0.484}{18}=0.0540438126.\]
\[\mathrm{SE}=\sqrt{s_p^2\left(\frac1{9}+\frac1{11}\right)}=0.104488956,\qquad\nu=18.\]
\[\bar y-\bar x=0.22.\]

Under \(H_0\), the test statistic has a \(t_{18}\) distribution.

\[t=\frac{\text{sample estimate}-\text{null value}}{\mathrm{SE}}=\frac{0.22-(0)}{0.10448896}=2.105.\]

The 5% one-sided rejection region is \(t\ge 1.734\).

Since \(2.105\ge 1.734\), reject \(H_0\). There is sufficient evidence at the 5% level that algorithm B has a greater population mean segment duration than algorithm A.

questions.title: Pooling centred sums for an interval
questions.prompt_html:
The durations of two finishing processes are measured in minutes. Two independent random samples are taken: 9 observations from population A and 11 from population B. The observations are denoted by x and y, respectively.

Population A sample

\[\sum x=163.8,\qquad\sum(x-\bar{x})^2=18.\]

Population B sample

\[\sum y=191.4,\qquad\sum(y-\bar{y})^2=32.4.\]

Assume that both populations are normal with the same unknown variance.

Write \(\mu_A\) and \(\mu_B\) for the two population means, in the stated units.

  1. Find a 95% confidence interval for \(\mu_A-\mu_B\), giving both endpoints to 3 decimal places.

    [6]

  2. Use your interval to state the conclusion of a two-sided 5% test of equality of the population means. Explain your reasoning.

    [1]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\((-0.780,\ 2.380)\) minutes.

(b)

Zero lies in the interval. Therefore the matching two-sided test does not provide sufficient evidence that the population means differ. This does not prove that the population means are equal.
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Using the unbiased variance estimate,

\[\bar{x}=\frac{163.8}{9}=18.2,\]
\[s^2=\frac{\sum x^2-(\sum x)^2/9}{8}=\frac{18}{8}=2.25.\]

Using the unbiased variance estimate,

\[\bar{y}=\frac{191.4}{11}=17.4,\]
\[s_y^2=\frac{\sum y^2-(\sum y)^2/11}{10}=\frac{32.4}{10}=3.24.\]
\[s_p^2=\frac{(8)s_x^2+(10)s_y^2}{18}=\frac{18+32.4}{18}=2.8.\]
\[\mathrm{SE}=\sqrt{s_p^2\left(\frac1{9}+\frac1{11}\right)}=0.752101433,\qquad\nu=18.\]

Use an equal-tailed 95% confidence interval for \(\mu_A-\mu_B\).

\[t_{18,0.975}\approx 2.101,\qquad\text{interval}=\text{estimate}\pm c\,\mathrm{SE}.\]
\[0.8\pm 2.100922\times 0.75210143=0.8\pm 1.5801065.\]

The interval is \((-0.780,\ 2.380)\) minutes.

The population variance is unknown: using a standard normal critical value instead of the \(t\) critical value would not be the specified small-sample procedure.

(b)

Zero lies in the interval. Therefore the matching two-sided test does not provide sufficient evidence that the population means differ. This does not prove that the population means are equal.

questions.title: Known variances: the normal procedure
questions.prompt_html:
Two independent normal populations have means \(\mu_X\) and \(\mu_Y\) and known population variances \(\sigma_X^2=10.24\) and \(\sigma_Y^2=14.44\). Independent random samples of sizes 16 and 25 give \(\bar x=24.8\) and \(\bar y=24.1\), respectively.

  1. Find a 90% confidence interval for \(\mu_X-\mu_Y\), giving both endpoints to 3 decimal places.

    [4]

  2. Explain why a t critical value is not required even though the samples are small.

    [1]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\((-1.115,\ 2.515)\).

(b)

The populations are normal and their variances are known. Therefore the standardised difference of the sample means is exactly standard normal; neither a pooled variance estimate nor a t critical value is required.
questions.solution_html:

The population variances are known, so they are not estimated from these samples.

\[\mathrm{SE}=\sqrt{\frac{10.24}{16}+\frac{14.44}{25}}=1.10344914.\]

\[z_{0.95}\approx 1.645,\qquad\text{interval}=\text{estimate}\pm c\,\mathrm{SE}.\]
\[0.7\pm 1.644854\times 1.1034491=0.7\pm 1.8150123.\]

The interval is \((-1.115,\ 2.515)\).

Here the interval uses the exact normal distribution because both populations are normal and their variances are known.

(b)

questions.title: Why unequal variances need not be pooled
questions.prompt_html:
The time to carry out a routine check is measured in minutes at two sites. Two independent random samples are taken: 40 observations from population A and 60 from population B. The observations are denoted by x and y, respectively.

Population A sample

\[\sum x=254,\qquad\sum x^2=1678.81.\]

Population B sample

\[\sum y=367.2,\qquad\sum y^2=2380.014.\]

The population variances are finite and need not be equal. Use a large-sample normal approximation.

Write \(\mu_A\) and \(\mu_B\) for the two population means, in the stated units.

  1. Find a 90% confidence interval for \(\mu_A-\mu_B\), giving both endpoints to 3 decimal places.

    [5]

  2. Explain why your interval does not require equal population variances.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\((-0.235,\ 0.695)\) minutes.

(b)

The squared standard error is estimated by \(s_A^2/n_A+s_B^2/n_B\). It does not assume a common population variance, so pooling is neither required nor justified by the sample sizes alone.
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Using the unbiased variance estimate,

\[\bar{x}=\frac{254}{40}=6.35,\]
\[s^2=\frac{\sum x^2-(\sum x)^2/40}{39}=\frac{65.91}{39}=1.69.\]

Using the unbiased variance estimate,

\[\bar{y}=\frac{367.2}{60}=6.12,\]
\[s_y^2=\frac{\sum y^2-(\sum y)^2/60}{59}=\frac{132.75}{59}=2.25.\]

The samples are large and independent. Use the normal approximation to the difference of sample means, with separate variance estimates; do not pool.

\[\mathrm{SE}=\sqrt{\frac{s_x^2}{40}+\frac{s_y^2}{60}}=0.282400425.\]

Use an equal-tailed 90% confidence interval for \(\mu_A-\mu_B\).

\[z_{0.95}\approx 1.645,\qquad\text{interval}=\text{estimate}\pm c\,\mathrm{SE}.\]
\[0.23\pm 1.644854\times 0.28240042=0.23\pm 0.46450736.\]

The interval is \((-0.235,\ 0.695)\) minutes.

This interval uses the large-sample normal approximation, with separate estimates of the two population variances.

(b)

The squared standard error is estimated by \(s_A^2/n_A+s_B^2/n_B\). It does not assume a common population variance, so pooling is neither required nor justified by the sample sizes alone.

(a)
